transcribes.note: PRINTED AT LENGTH AND NOT MERELY CITED. At pages 34-35 the volume introduces the Kinzie and Clybourn genealogy as 'best told by Rufus Blanchard ... He says:' and sets the whole passage as a block quotation, which is why bk_mose1_019 - Benjamin Hall's 1830 arrival and the town's first tannery - is a reading of Blanchard through Moses and Kirkland and not of Moses and Kirkland. This project does not hold Blanchard and cannot check the transcription. Blanchard in turn credits Benjamin Hall himself for the detail, so the chain to the fact is three deep and the claim says so.

The full row-by-row result is committed at data/research/books/moses_kirkland_v1_lead_surnames.json so the next run does not pay for the search twice.

VOLUME 2, WHICH IS HALF THE WORK. Only volume 1 is read. The Newberry cards do not say which volume they cite, so an absence recorded here may simply be in the other book, and every ABSENT verdict in the lookup file says so on itself.

AN INDEPENDENT VOICE. It is a compilation of 1895 and it names its own authorities on the pages read: Andreas for Garrett's $1,800,000 of auction sales, Bross's History of Chicago page 38 for the earliest deeds, the Story of Chicago page 130 for Caton's election tally, Hurlbut's Chicago Antiquities pages 37-8 for the pre-1830 settler list, S. R. Beggs's West and Northwest page 95 for the Black Hawk alarm, and Rufus Blanchard's Discovery of the Northwest and History of Chicago (1881) quoted at length for the Kinzie-Clybourn genealogy. Where the sentence itself credits another work, the claim says so and the citation must go to that work and not to this one.
A SINGLE ADDRESS IN THE MODERN SENSE, and no street numbers. Positions here are corners, lots, blocks, a river bank and a tree.

ANY DATE FINER THAN THE YEAR for two things this project wanted finer: Caton's marriage, which is given as '1835' with the scene date sitting in the middle of it, and the Hubbard-Marsh packing partnership, which is 'later'.

CONSISTENCY WITH ITSELF. Page 89 dates Dole's and Peck's first frame business buildings to 1832 while page 570 has Peck's occupied in the fall of 1831; page 207 forms the Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company on 7 October 1835 while page 570 has it organised on 20 October 1835. Both readings of each are recorded and neither is adopted.
what_it_supplies: A TRADE CENSUS OF THE WHOLE TOWN, at page 95: the State census taken between 1 September and December 1835 counted 3,297 people, forty-four stores, two book stores, four druggists, two silversmiths and jewellers, two tin and copper manufactories, two printing offices, two breweries, one steam saw-mill, one iron foundry, four storage and forwarding houses, eight taverns, one lottery office, one bank, five churches, seven schools, twenty-two lawyers, fourteen physicians, and a lyceum and reading room. The project had no denominator for its business layer and this is one - for December 1835 and not for July.

A BUILDING WITH FOUR OF THE FIVE FIELDS data/structures/ WANTS, at page 90: John S. C. Hogan's story-and-a-half log storehouse, 45 by 18 feet, at the angle where Lake and South Water streets meet, with the post office partitioned off inside it from 2 November 1832.

TWO RESIDENCES STATED AS SUCH, which is the field the town is thinnest in: Rev. Jeremiah Porter lodging and keeping his study in the second storey of Peck's store from May 1833 (page 571), and John Dean Caton renting the back room and attic of Dr Temple's Temple Building from December 1833, sleeping in the attic and practising law in the back room, and sub-letting desk-room in it to his competitor Spring (page 577).

BUSINESSES GIVEN BY CORNER, LOT OR LANDMARK: Dole's and Peck's first frame business buildings at the south-east corners of South Water and Dearborn and of South Water and La Salle (page 89); Peck's two-storey frame store of black walnut brought from Detroit, occupied in the fall of 1831 (page 570); Sylvester Marsh killing beef under an old elm on the open prairie at what became Monroe Street from the winter of 1833-4 (page 389); William Jones's lots 2 and 7 in block 17 fronting Water and Lake (page 542).

OCCUPATIONS AND ARRIVALS for men this project already holds: Philo Carpenter as the town's first druggist, arriving within a month before 19 August 1832; Benjamin Hall as proprietor of the first tannery ever established there, arriving 1830; Dole, Clybourn, the Noble brothers and Gurdon S. Hubbard beginning the slaughtering and packing trade in 1832; the 1833 spring arrivals including Caton, Kimball and Asahel Pierce; and Hubbard's permanent residence dated to 1832 by the compiler's own reason for leaving him off a list.

TWO PRESENCE LISTS: the twenty-two men who signed the Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company roll on 7 October 1835 (pages 207-208), and, unread and left for its own ticket, the 'LIST OF ACTUAL SETTLERS AT CHICAGO, PRIOR TO 1830' at pages 78-79, about thirty rows with nativity, year and remarks columns.
ONE STATEMENT ABOUT THE GROUND OF THE SCENE, at page 79: the winter of 1834-5 was open, with little snow, front doors standing open all winter, and cattle living on grass on the river bank.

content_warning: 18+. Graphic violence from the eyewitness accounts: men and women shot, stabbed and struck down with tomahawks and the dead scalped, staged in the scenes; the worst mutilations described in the narration. No child is shown being killed.

endings.text: 16 August 1812. 'The next morning, they set fire to the fort and left the place, taking the prisoners with them.' Only the brick magazine 'alone defied the fire'. On the third day the Kinzies were put into a boat for St. Joseph. Heald and his wife were taken there too, and the scattered prisoners were held in the villages 'until the following spring, when they were, for the most part, carried to Detroit and ransomed'. The army came back in 1816 and built the second Fort Dearborn on the same ground. Quaife's warning about Wau-Bun, the family's book that shaped this story for a century: its accounts do Heald 'grave injustice'.

evidence.locator: p. 43, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 6876-6890 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected: Heald's letter of 15 April 1812)
evidence.text: Captain Nathan Heald, writing from Chicago on 15 April 1812: 'On the 6th instant, a little before sunset, a party of eleven Indians, supposed to be Winnebagoes, came to Messrs. Russell and Lee's cabin, in a field on the Portage branch of the Chicago river, about three miles from the garrison, where they murdered two men, one by the name of Liberty White, an American, and the other a Canadian Frenchman whose name I do not know.' The 1895 editors add the name [Debou] in brackets.

evidence.locator: ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text, the April section; ch. XIX for the boy as Lee's son
evidence.text: Wau-Bun dates the attack to the 7th and tells the escape. A discharged soldier and a boy (Lee's son, by ch. XIX) left the visitors in the cabin and walked to the two canoes tied by the bank. The soldier 'pointed to the cattle which were standing among the haystacks on the opposite bank, and made signs that they must go and fodder them'. Once across, hidden by the haystacks, 'they took to the woods' and made for the fort, hearing two shots behind them. Their story: the farm was 'occupied by a Mr. White and three persons employed by him'.

evidence.locator: ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text, the April section
evidence.text: Wau-Bun: running down the river the two fugitives 'arrived opposite Burns's, where, as before related, they called across to advertise the family of their danger, and then hastened on to the fort.' Ensign Ronan volunteered with five or six soldiers: 'They ascended the river in a scow, and took the mother, with her infant of scarcely a day old, upon her bed to the boat'. A corporal and six men were fishing upriver, so 'the commanding officer ordered a cannon to be fired, to warn them of danger.'

evidence.reasoning: Heald's letter of 15 April 1812 gives the arrival at the cabin as a little before sunset and the distance as about three miles; Wau-Bun has the runners call across to Burns's on their way down to the fort. Nobody wrote down the hour of the warning, so dusk is the reading of those two facts, not a found time.
evidence.text: The two runners left the cabin after the visitors came, which Heald puts a little before sunset, and ran some three miles down the river, stopping opposite the Burns house on the way; this stop is set at dusk. The hour is not recorded.

evidence.locator: Quaife, the chapter on the first fort (Gutenberg #69274 plain text, the paragraph on the civilians around the fort); Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text
evidence.text: Quaife (1913): 'after the murders at the Lee farm, Captain Heald enrolled fifteen militiamen from the civilian population outside the fort.' Wau-Bun: the people outside the fort 'now intrenched themselves in the Agency House'; its piazzas 'were planked up, for greater security, port-holes were cut, and sentinels posted at night.'

evidence.locator: note 583, Gutenberg #69274 plain text, the evacuation chapter
evidence.text: General William Hull's order, Sandwich, 29 July 1812, found among the Heald papers and first printed by Quaife: 'It is with regret I order the Evacuation of your Post owing to the want of Provisions only a neglect of the Commandant' ... 'You will therefore Destroy all arms & ammunition, but the Goods of the Factory you may give to the Friendly Indians who may be desirous of Escorting you on to Fort Wayne & to the Poor & needy of your Post.'

evidence.locator: Quaife Appendix III (Heald's journal) and the evacuation chapter; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text
evidence.text: Heald's journal: 'On the 9th of Augt, 1812, rec'd orders from Genl Wm. Hull to evacuate the Post of Chicago and proceed with my Command to Detroit.' Quaife: 'The next day the Indian runner. Winnemac, delivered to Captain Heald at Fort Dearborn his order for the evacuation.' Wau-Bun puts the runner, Winnemeg or Catfish, a Potawatomi, at the post on the 7th, bringing despatches that 'announced the declaration of war between the United States and Great Britain'. Wau-Bun: 'The order for evacuating the post was read next morning upon parade', and the officers' 'unanimous advice was, to remain where they were, and fortify themselves as strongly as possible.' Quaife defends Heald: 'Obedience to orders is the primary duty of a soldier.'

evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Quaife note 589 and the evacuation chapter; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text
evidence.text: Heald's report: 'The neighboring Indians got the information as early as I did, and came in from all quarters in order to receive the goods in the factory store, which they understood were to be given them.' His warriors on the 15th were 'mostly of the Potawatamie nation' (the Potawatomi, as the name is now written). Wau-Bun puts a council on the afternoon of the 12th: 'Captain Heald alone attended on the part of the military.' His officers 'took command of the block-houses which overlooked the esplanade on which the council was held, opened the port-holes, and pointed the cannon so as to command the whole assembly.' Quaife thinks the council was 'probably' on the 13th.

evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text
evidence.text: Heald's report: 'On the 14th, I delivered the Indians all the goods in the factory store, and a considerable quantity of provisions which we could not take away with us.' Wau-Bun, which dates it the 13th: 'the goods, consisting of blankets, broadcloths, calicoes, paints, etc., were distributed, as stipulated.'

evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text
evidence.text: Heald's report: 'The surplus arms and ammunition I thought proper to destroy, fearing they would make bad use of it if put in their possession. I also destroyed all the liquor on hand after they began to collect.' Wau-Bun: 'The same evening the ammunition and liquor were carried, part into the sally-port, and thrown into a well which had been dug there to supply the garrison with water in case of emergency; the remainder was transported as secretly as possible through the northern gate, the heads of the barrels knocked in, and the contents poured into the river.' The muskets 'were broken up and thrown into the well'. The noise betrayed it, and 'the taste of the water the next morning was, as one expressed it, "strong grog."'

evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Quaife, the evacuation chapter; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text
evidence.text: Heald's report: 'On the 13th, Captain Wells, of Fort Wayne, arrived with about 30 Miamies, for the purpose of escorting us in, by the request of General Hull.' Wau-Bun has him arrive on the 14th 'with fifteen friendly Miamis' to save 'his relative, Captain Heald', and says he came 'all too late': the ammunition was already destroyed. Quaife: Heald's wife Rebekah was 'the niece of Captain Wells'.

evidence.locator: ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text; Quaife, the evacuation chapter and note 591
evidence.text: Wau-Bun: on the evening after the second council 'Black Partridge, a conspicuous chief, entered the quarters of the commanding officer' and gave back his medal: 'I will not wear a token of peace while I am compelled to act as an enemy.' Quaife: Black Partridge was 'a Pottawatomie chief from the Illinois River' (a Potawatomi leader); of the two contemporary versions, Lieutenant Helm's and Sergeant Griffith's through McAfee, both record his warning and 'Helm alone mentions the surrender of the medal.'

evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Quaife, the battle chapter; Wau-Bun ch. XIX, Narrative of the Massacre, Continued, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text
evidence.text: Heald's report: 'On the 15th, at 9 o'clock in the morning, we commenced our march: a part of the Miamies were detached in front, and the remainder in our rear, as guards, under the direction of Captain Wells. The situation of the country rendered it necessary for us to take the beach, with the lake on our left, and a high sand bank on our right, at about 100 yards distance.' Wau-Bun: 'As the troops left the fort, the band struck up the Dead March', and Wells 'had blackened his face before leaving the garrison, in token of his impending fate.' Mrs. Kinzie's boat 'had scarcely reached the mouth of the river, which, it will be recollected, was here half a mile below the fort, when another messenger from To-pee-nee-bee arrived to detain them where they were.' Quaife lists the order: Wells and part of the Miamis, the garrison, the women and children, the twelve Chicago militia.

evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Quaife, the battle chapter and note 596
evidence.text: Heald's report: 'We had proceeded about a mile and a half, when it was discovered that the Indians were prepared to attack us from behind the bank. I immediately marched up with the company to the top of the bank, when the action commenced; after firing one round, we charged, and the Indians gave way in front and joined those on our flanks.' Quaife: 'Meanwhile a deadlier combat, which we may perhaps think of as a separate battle, was raging around the wagons in the rear.' The militia 'were cut down to a man'. Among the dead were 'Cicely, Mrs. Heald's negro serving-woman' and 'her infant son, who also perished', two of the few recorded people held in slavery at Chicago.

evidence.locator: Appendix III, Nathan Heald's Journal, Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text
evidence.text: Captain Heald's journal: 'On the 15th Marched for Detroit & was attacked by about 500 Indians two miles from the Fort'.

evidence.locator: Appendix VI, Lieutenant Helm's account of the massacre, Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text (Quaife's '[a]' is his insertion)
evidence.text: Lieutenant Helm's account (1814): 'we evacuated the Garrison & about one and [a] half mile from the Garrison we were informed by Capt Wells that we were surrounded & the attack by the Indians began, about 10 of the Clock Morning'.

evidence.locator: Andreas, History of Chicago vol. 1 (1884), p. 31, Arnold to Andreas, 25 January 1884 (the OCR's 'light' read as 'fight'); Kirkland, The Chicago Massacre of 1812 (1893), Fernando Jones's letter, Project Gutenberg eBook #59624 plain text
evidence.text: Isaac N. Arnold, 1884, of the Eighteenth Street cottonwood: 'This tree was pointed out to me by both Mr. and Mrs. Kinzie, as near the place where the attack began. As the fight continued the combatants moved south and west over considerable space.' Fernando Jones, who came in 1835, 'visited many times the location of the Indian massacre of 1812. The spot was pointed out by some who were children at the time, and by others who had been informed by their parents.'

evidence.reasoning: T-3469 (the owner's choice, 2026-11-07). Heald's report gives about a mile and a half, a straight line to the later Roosevelt Road; his journal gives two miles, near Seventeenth Street; Arnold, from the Kinzies, puts the start of the attack at the Eighteenth Street tree, and Fernando Jones was shown the ground and the burials near Seventeenth and Prairie. The stand is where those meet; the scene card 'Where the attack happened' keeps the Roosevelt Road reading beside it.
evidence.text: This stand is on the reconstructed 1812 beach just south of the later Eighteenth Street, about 60 m south of the two Eighteenth Street cottonwoods, looking north-north-west up the shore with the high sand bank of terrain_spec.json battle_bank_1812 and its cottonwoods on the left; it follows the readings that name a place, not a marked spot.

evidence.reasoning: data/terrain/epochs/e1830_natural/terrain_spec.json heald_small_elevation_1812: centred at local E 1215, N -3420, 377 m from the water on its row, beyond the high bank and the ravine of battle_bank_1812. South-west because Arnold, from the Kinzies, has the fight moving 'south and west', Wau-Bun has the rising ground 'not far from the Oak Woods', which lay south, and Fernando Jones's vidette grave at Twenty-first and Indiana lay 'southwest of the massacre-ground'. Moved by T-3469; admitted in docs/LIBERTIES.md L-t3403-battle-shore-1812.
evidence.text: This stand is on the open prairie just below a rise placed for Heald's 'small elevation in the open prarie, out of shot of the bank or any other cover', south-west of the Eighteenth Street bank near the later Nineteenth Street and Indiana Avenue; the accounts give no distance or size, so its place and height are this reconstruction's.

evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text
evidence.text: Heald's report: he 'took possession of a small elevation in the open prarie, out of shot of the bank or any other cover' and was met 'by one of the Potawatamie chiefs, called the Black Bird' (a Potawatomi leader), who 'requested me to surrender, promising to spare the lives of all the prisoners.' The toll he gives: 'twenty-six regulars and all the militia were killed in the action, with two women and twelve children. Ensign George Ronan and doctor Isaac V Van Voorhis of my company, with Captain Wells, of Fort Wayne, are, to my great sorrow, numbered among the dead.' The warriors numbered 'between four and five hundred', and their loss 'was about fifteen.' The report opens: 'I embrace this opportunity to render you an account of the garrison of Chicago.'

evidence.locator: ch. XIX, Narrative of the Massacre, Continued, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text
evidence.text: Wau-Bun: Mrs. Heald, badly wounded, was ransomed by Kinzie's clerk Chandonnai for a mule and the promise of whiskey and brought to the boat, and then to the house, where 'Mr. Kinzie then performed the operation himself, with his penknife.' 'At their own mansion the family of Mr. Kinzie were closely guarded by their Indian friends.' On the 16th 'Black Partridge, Wau-ban-see, and Kee-po-tah, with two other Indians' sat in the porch as sentinels. A party from the Wabash, who had 'blackened their faces', came into the parlor and 'seated themselves upon the floor in silence'. Then Billy Caldwell, the Sauganash, 'entered the parlor with a calm step', laid his rifle behind the door and greeted them as friends; 'thus taken by surprise', they 'said modestly that they came to beg of their friends some white cotton in which to wrap their dead before interring them.'

evidence.locator: ch. XIX, Narrative of the Massacre, Continued, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text; Kirkland 1893, the opening chapter, footnote [A] (Gutenberg #59624 plain text, line 590); Quaife Appendix II, on Mrs. Helm's narrative
evidence.text: Wau-Bun: Black Partridge had Mrs. Helm put on 'the ordinary dress of a Frenchwoman of the country' and led her to Ouilmette's house. When the searchers came, the household 'raised a large feather bed and placed her under the edge of it, upon the bedstead, with her face to the wall', and Mrs. Bisson, the sister of Ouilmette's wife, 'seated herself with her sewing upon the front of the bed.' Nearly suffocating, Mrs. Helm begged to be given up: 'I can but die,' said she; 'let them put an end to my misery at once.' The searchers looked about the room 'and left the house.' Quaife (1913) warns that this part of Wau-Bun may be heightened: 'That Black Partridge saved Mrs. Helm is probably true, but that the affair possessed the romantic aspect which it has come to assume in the popular mind ... seems unlikely.' Her first name is in Kirkland (1893): 'Margaret Helm, wife of Lieutenant Helm, and step-daughter of old John Kinzie'.

evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Quaife, the description of the fort and the evacuation chapter; Wau-Bun ch. XIX, Narrative of the Massacre, Continued, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text
evidence.text: Heald's report: 'The next morning, they set fire to the fort and left the place, taking the prisoners with them.' Quaife: the magazine, 'a small structure made of brick', 'alone defied the fire'. Wau-Bun: 'On the third day after the battle, the family of Mr. Kinzie, with the clerks of the establishment, were put into a boat' for St. Joseph. The prisoners, Wau-Bun says, were dispersed among the villages 'until the following spring, when they were, for the most part, carried to Detroit and ransomed'; Mrs. Lee and her infant were taken to Black Partridge's village on the Au Sable, and Mrs. Burns 'with her infant, became the prisoner of a chief'. Heald's journal: 'On the 16th, that is the day after [the] action, Mrs. Heald & myself were taken to the St. Joseph River by our new Masters.' The army came back in 1816 and began the second fort on the same site (Quaife, the chapter on the second fort). Quaife on Wau-Bun as a whole: its accounts 'all proceed, directly or indirectly from a common source', and do Heald 'grave injustice'.

evidence.locator: Quaife, ch. VII, the paragraph beginning 'In March, 1811'; ch. X, the paragraph on Van Voorhis; Appendix IV, Heald's report
evidence.text: Quaife (1913): Ensign George Ronan was 'a young cadet direct from West Point', ordered to Fort Dearborn in March 1811; Lieutenant Linai T. Helm came from Detroit at his own request, for 'his straitened financial circumstances and the cheaper cost of living at Fort Dearborn as compared with Detroit.' Surgeon's mate Isaac Van Voorhis, writing in October 1811: 'In my solitary walks I contemplate what a great and powerful republic will yet arise in this new world. Here, I say, will be the seat of millions yet unborn'. Quaife: 'The man who at the age of twenty-two could pen these lines'. Heald's report: 'Ensign George Ronan and Doctor Isaac V. Van Voorhis of my company, with Captain Wells of Fort Wayne' were killed; Helm was taken prisoner.

evidence.locator: Quaife 1913, the chapters on the building of the fort, the garrison of 1810 and the evacuation, Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text
evidence.text: Quaife (1913): 'At half-past five o'clock on the morning of July 14, 1803, the troops set out from Detroit'; they 'reached the Chicago River at two o'clock on the afternoon of August 17'. The fort: 'The barracks and other structures for the accommodation of the garrison were built around the four sides of a quadrangle', with 'Two blockhouses' and 'a double row of palisades'. In April 1810 Captain John Whistler was moved to Detroit, and 'Captain Nathan Heald, who, in turn, succeeded Whistler at Fort Dearborn'. Heald's report: 'Our strength was fifty-four regulars and twelve militia'.

evidence.reasoning: Heald's letter of 15 April 1812 dates the attack at the cabin to the 6th, a little before sunset. The opening scene at the fort is set earlier that day so that the story begins before it; nobody wrote down an hour for it.
evidence.text: The story opens at the fort on the afternoon of 6 April 1812, the day Heald's letter puts the killings at Lee's Place 'a little before sunset'. The hour is not recorded; afternoon is the stop's setting.

evidence.locator: Wau-Bun, the April section; the Reader, the sutler paragraph; Kirkland, the Helm narrative
evidence.text: Wau-Bun (1856): 'On the north side of the main stream, but quite near its junction with Lake Michigan, stood (as has already been described) the dwelling-house and trading-establishment of Mr. Kinzie.' 'The fort was situated on the southern bank, directly opposite this mansion'. The Chicago Reader (2018): in January 1812 Heald made 'Messrs. Kinzie & Forsyth' the exclusive fort sutlers. Kirkland (1893): Margaret Helm was the 'step-daughter of old John Kinzie'.

evidence.locator: Currey, ch. on Lee's Place, Project Gutenberg plain text lines 1455-1540; Wau-Bun, ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text
evidence.text: Currey (1912): 'Lee's place was also known as "Hardscrabble," a name which continued to be applied to that neighborhood for many decades thereafter.' The farm 'was owned by a man named Charles Lee, who, however, did not live on the premises, but occupied a house near the fort.' 'On the seventh of April of the fateful year 1812 the log house at Hardscrabble was occupied by three men and a boy. The man who seems to have been in charge of the work at the farm was one Liberty White, and with him were a discharged soldier, also a Frenchman named Debou, and the boy, a son of Mr. Lee's.' 'The products of the farm found a ready market at the fort'. Wau-Bun: 'Lee's Place, since known by the name of Hardscrabble, was a farm intersected by the Chicago River, about four miles from its mouth.'

evidence.locator: Currey, ch. on Lee's Place, Project Gutenberg plain text lines 1455-1540
evidence.text: Currey (1912): that afternoon 'a party of soldiers from the fort, consisting of a corporal and six men, had obtained leave to go up the river to catch a supply of fish'. They passed Lee's place 'with the usual exchange of greetings' and fished two miles beyond 'until nearly dark. Suddenly they were startled by hearing the dull boom of a cannon'. Coming back, they found the place 'silent and deserted', stumbled on a body, and reached the fort 'about eleven o'clock at night'.

evidence.locator: Quaife 1913, the chapters on the building of the fort, the garrison of 1810 and the evacuation, Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text
evidence.text: Quaife (1913): on 28 July 1812 'two Chippewa Indians reached Hull's camp at Sandwich bringing news of the surrender of Mackinac.' On 29 July Hull wrote, 'I shall immediately send an express to Fort Dearborn with orders to evacuate that post'. Hull was the American general commanding at Detroit.

evidence.reasoning: Heald's own date for the order's arrival plus Wau-Bun's 'next morning' for its reading; the two sources differ by two days on the runner, so the date is a reading, not a record.
evidence.text: Heald's journal has the order received on 9 August; Wau-Bun says it 'was read next morning upon parade'. This stop is set on the morning of 10 August, putting the two together; the hour is Wau-Bun's 'next morning', not a recorded time.

evidence.reasoning: Wau-Bun's sequence on the 13th (goods, then 'The same evening' the well); Heald dates the goods to the 14th. The hour is the jaunt's, inside the daylight the sequence needs.
evidence.text: Wau-Bun puts the goods out on the 13th and the powder down the well 'The same evening', so the giving-out was by day; this stop is set at two in the afternoon of the 13th. No hour is recorded.

evidence.reasoning: Wau-Bun's 'evening succeeding the council' and the march next morning; the hour is a reading of 'evening'.
evidence.text: Wells reached the fort on the 13th by Heald's report or the 14th by Wau-Bun; Black Partridge came to the commanding officer 'on the evening' after the second council. This stop is set at sunset on 14 August, the eve of the march.

evidence.reasoning: Sequence in Heald's report (charge, withdrawal to 'a small elevation in the open prarie', parley, surrender) after an attack Helm puts at about ten; an estimate.
evidence.text: The fight at the bank, the struggle at the wagons and Heald's withdrawal to the rise all came before the surrender; this stop is set at half past ten that morning. No source gives the hour.

evidence.reasoning: Moses and Kirkland p. 60 and Andreas p. 31 for the tradition; the planting massacre_cottonwoods_1812 for the trees' places (L372). Heald's report's mile and a half falls short of them, his journal's two miles near them.
evidence.text: Two cottonwoods in the later Eighteenth Street were remembered as the place of the attack, a tradition written down from the 1880s and carried by the Kinzie family; this scene stands them where it put them, and since T-3469 the battle stops stand beside them.

evidence.reasoning: Wau-Bun's sequence: boat held at the river mouth during the fight, the family taken home after it; the hour is the jaunt's.
evidence.text: Wau-Bun has the Kinzies returned to their own house after the battle and Mrs. Heald brought there; this stop is set at sunset on 15 August. The Wabash party and Billy Caldwell came the next day. No hour is recorded.

evidence.reasoning: Heald's 'The next morning, they set fire to the fort' and Wau-Bun's placing of the search on the day after the battle; the hour is an estimate.
evidence.text: Wau-Bun sets the search of Ouilmette's house on the 16th, the day the fort was burned 'The next morning'; this stop is set at nine that morning. No hour is recorded.

evidence.locator: ch. II, Building of the First Fort Dearborn, Captain Heald's letter of 15 April 1812, Project Gutenberg eBook #59624 plain text lines 2305-2319
evidence.text: Captain Heald's letter from Chicago, 15 April 1812, as Kirkland prints it: 'White received two balls through his body, nine stabs with a knife in his breast, and one in his hip, his throat was cut from ear to ear, his nose and lips were taken off in one piece, and his head was skinned almost as far round as they could find any hair. The Frenchman was only shot through the neck and scalped.'

evidence.locator: ch. II, Building of the First Fort Dearborn, the condensation of Mrs. Kinzie's narrative, Project Gutenberg eBook #59624 plain text lines 2255-2300
evidence.text: Mrs. Kinzie's narrative of the attack at Lee's place, as Kirkland condenses it: the soldier and the boy 'had run a quarter of a mile when they heard the discharge of two guns successively.' That night the fishing party stopped to warn the house: 'as the corporal jumped over the small enclosure he placed his hand on the dead body of a man. By the sense of touch he soon ascertained that the head was without a scalp and was otherwise mutilated. The faithful dog of the murdered man stood guarding the remains of his master.'

evidence.locator: Part I, Margaret Helm's Story, Project Gutenberg eBook #59624 plain text lines 764-790
evidence.text: Margaret Helm's story (Wau-Bun), as Kirkland reprints it: 'Captain Wells, who had kept somewhat in advance of his Miamis, came riding furiously back. "They are about to attack us!" he shouted. "Form instantly and charge upon them." Scarcely were the words uttered when a volley was showered from among the sand-hills. The troops were hastily brought into line and charged up the bank. One man, a veteran of seventy winters, fell as they ascended.' 'The troops behaved most gallantly. They were but a handful, but they seemed resolved to sell their lives as dearly as possible.'

evidence.locator: ch. V, Fate of the Fugitives, Project Gutenberg eBook #59624 plain text lines 3315-3330
evidence.text: Wau-Bun's account of Nau-non-gee, a chief of the Calumet village, as Kirkland reprints it: 'During the battle of the 15th of August, the chief object of his attack was one Sergeant Hays, a man from whom he had received many acts of kindness. After Hays had received a ball through the body, this Indian ran up to tomahawk him, when the Sergeant, collecting his remaining strength, pierced him through the body with his bayonet. They fell together. Other Indians running up soon dispatched Hays, and it was not until then that his bayonet was extracted from the body of his adversary.' The wounded chief was carried to his village on the Calumet and survived several days.

evidence.locator: Part I, Margaret Helm's Story, Project Gutenberg eBook #59624 plain text lines 795-850
evidence.text: Margaret Helm's story (Wau-Bun), as Kirkland reprints it: the surgeon 'was badly wounded. His horse was shot under him and he had received a ball in his leg.' 'I pointed to Ensign Ronan, who, though mortally wounded and nearly down, was still fighting with desperation on one knee.' 'At this moment a young Indian raised his tomahawk at me. By springing aside I avoided the blow, which was intended for my skull, but which alighted on my shoulder. I seized him around the neck, and while exerting my utmost efforts to get possession of his scalping-knife, which hung in a scabbard over his breast, I was dragged from his grasp by another and an older Indian. The latter bore me struggling and resisting toward the lake.' She passed 'the remains of the unfortunate surgeon. Some murderous tomahawk had stretched him upon the very spot where I had last seen him.' 'I was immediately plunged into the water and held there with a forcible hand'; her captor kept her head above water, and she knew him, 'in spite of the paint with which he was disguised', as The Black Partridge.

evidence.locator: Part I, after Rebekah Heald's Story, Project Gutenberg eBook #59624 plain text lines 1280-1295
evidence.text: Margaret Helm's story (Wau-Bun), as Kirkland reprints it: 'But in the meantime, a horrible scene had been enacted. One young savage, climbing into the baggage-wagon containing the children of the white families, twelve in number, tomahawked the children of the entire group.' Kirkland takes it as confirmed by Heald's count of the dead, 'two women and twelve children'.

evidence.locator: Part I, Death of Captain Wells, Project Gutenberg eBook #59624 plain text lines 1043-1070
evidence.text: Rebekah Heald's story, taken down by Kirkland from her son Darius Heald in 1892: 'Captain Wells, who was shot through the lungs, rode up and took her hand, saying: "Farewell my child."' 'He told her he was shot through the lungs, and she saw the blood oozing through his nose and mouth.' 'His horse, which had been shot just behind the girth, then fell and caught Captain Wells' leg under him. As he did so, Captain Wells turned and saw six or seven Indians approaching them. He took aim and fired, killing one of them.' 'Mrs. Heald said to him: "Uncle, there is an Indian pointing right at the back of your head." Captain Wells put his hand back and held up his head that better aim might be taken, and then cried "Shoot away!" The Indian fired, the shot being fatal. They then pulled him out from under his horse (Mrs. Heald still seated on her horse near by) and cut his body open, the gashes being in the shape of a cross. They took out his heart'.

evidence.locator: Appendix G, Important Reminiscences of an Old Settler (A. H. Edwards), Project Gutenberg eBook #59624 plain text lines 6585-6700
evidence.text: A. H. Edwards to John Wentworth, 24 May 1891, from what a survivor told him, a soldier's daughter who rode in the wagons: she 'had been scalped'. 'She said a young Indian came to the wagon where she was and grabbed her by the hair and pulled her out of the wagon, and she fought him the best she knew how, scratching and biting, till finally he threw her down and scalped her.' 'I do not know the first name of Cooper. He was killed and the girl said she saw her father's scalp in the hands of an Indian afterward.'

evidence.locator: Part I, Margaret Helm's Story, Project Gutenberg eBook #59624 plain text lines 884-892
evidence.text: Margaret Helm's story (Wau-Bun), as Kirkland reprints it: led from the lake, she was 'Supported partly by my kind conductor, Black Partridge, and partly by another Indian, Pee-so-tum, who held dangling in his hand a scalp which, by the black ribbon around the queue, I recognized as that of Captain Wells'.

evidence.locator: Part I, Rebekah Heald's Story, Project Gutenberg eBook #59624 plain text lines 1026-1034
evidence.text: Rebekah Heald's story, through her son Darius: 'Just before the surrender, she got up in range of the bullets coming from Indians on both sides of her. She did not know whether the Indians aimed at her or not, but she was wounded in six places, one hand being rendered helpless, the ball passing between the two bones of her arm.'

keepsake.text: 'I embrace this opportunity to render you an account of the garrison of Chicago.' The commander's own account of the evacuation, written ten weeks after it.

opening.text:
JAUNT: THE BATTLE OF FORT DEARBORN, 18+. Spring 1812, where the Chicago River meets Lake Michigan. The nearest American post is Fort Wayne, far to the south-east; Detroit, where the general commands, is farther still. War with Britain is coming, and every report that reaches the fort makes it feel smaller and farther from help.

This telling is 18+. It walks the same thirteen stops as the students' jaunt, but at Lee's Place, on the beach and on the prairie the killing is staged as the people who lived through it described it: shots fired, knives and tomahawks used, men and women struck down, the dead scalped, and soldiers fighting back with the bayonet. The worst of what was done to the bodies is told, not shown, and no child is shown being harmed.

Thirteen stops in date order, with the time of day and the season set for each. Long rides go Instantly; every place keeps its stop.

The story begins with the fort, on the afternoon of 6 April 1812.

premise: 18+: 6 April to 16 August 1812 in thirteen stops, with the killings at Lee's Place, the attack on the beach and the death of Captain Wells staged as the witnesses described them.

stops.text: 6 April 1812, afternoon, before the fort. This story begins here. In the summer of 1803 Captain John Whistler's company marched in from Detroit and built it in logs: barracks round a small parade, 'Two blockhouses' and 'a double row of palisades'. It has stood for nine years. Since 1810 it has been commanded by Captain Nathan Heald, with fifty-four regular soldiers. Across the river lives John Kinzie, the trader who supplies the garrison, with his family and his clerks; his stepdaughter Margaret is married to the fort's lieutenant, Linai Helm. A handful of other families live along the banks: the Ouilmettes, the Burnses, and the hands at Charles Lee's farm. The situation is about to ignite, three miles up the river, a little before sunset.

stops.text: 6 April 1812, a little before sunset, at Lee's Place, later called Hardscrabble, up the South Branch. Eleven armed men walk into the log house and sit down; Captain Heald wrote that they were 'supposed to be Winnebagoes'. The soldier and Lee's young son slip across the river and run. Behind them comes 'the discharge of two guns successively.' Liberty White and the Canadian hand are shot down. Heald's letter lists what was done to White: 'two balls through his body, nine stabs with a knife in his breast, and one in his hip, his throat was cut from ear to ear, his nose and lips were taken off in one piece, and his head was skinned'. The Frenchman 'was only shot through the neck and scalped.' That night a soldier found the body, and 'The faithful dog of the murdered man stood guarding the remains of his master.'

stage.caption: Watch the Burns children answer the shouting, and Ensign Ronan's party carry their mother down to the boat.

stops.text: 6 April, dusk. Running downriver toward the fort, the two pause opposite this house, where the Burns family live, and shout across to warn them. At the fort Ensign George Ronan, 'a young cadet direct from West Point', takes five or six soldiers upriver in a flat-bottomed scow and brings Mrs. Burns out, 'with her infant of scarcely a day old, upon her bed to the boat'. A corporal and six men are still upriver fishing, so 'the commanding officer ordered a cannon to be fired'. They row home in the dark past the silent farm, find a scalped body by touch, and reach the gate about eleven at night. Heald enrols fifteen townsmen as militia. For four months the settlement waits behind its guns. When the blow comes, it comes as a letter.

stage.caption: Watch Captain Heald read the order to the company, and his officers come to argue against it.

stops.text: 10 August 1812, morning, on the parade. The United States has been at war with Britain since June, and the British have taken Mackinac, the American post up the lake. General William Hull, commanding at Detroit, sends a runner, Winnemac, with a written order for Captain Heald: 'It is with regret I order the Evacuation of your Post owing to the want of Provisions'. The arms are to be destroyed, and the goods in the government store given away. Wau-Bun says the order 'was read next morning upon parade', and that the officers' 'unanimous advice was, to remain where they were, and fortify themselves as strongly as possible.' Heald chooses to obey. Outside the pickets, hundreds of people have already heard, and are gathering to see what Heald will promise them.

stage.caption: Watch the council: Heald alone before the leaders, the gathering standing round, the blockhouse guns above.

stops.text: 12 August, afternoon (Quaife thinks the 13th), on this open ground outside the pickets. Heald wrote that the Potawatomi of the country round 'came in from all quarters in order to receive the goods in the factory store'. He meets their leaders in council here and promises them the goods. His own officers will not come: 'Captain Heald alone attended on the part of the military.' Instead they take the blockhouses that overlook this esplanade, open the port-holes and point the cannon 'so as to command the whole assembly.' It is a council held under the guns. He has promised the goods. He has not said what he means to do with the guns and the whiskey.

stage.caption: Watch the goods come out of the factory to the people of the gathering, while Heald looks on.

stops.text: 13 August, early afternoon. This log building is the factory, the government's trading house. Out of it now goes everything on the shelves: 'blankets, broadcloths, calicoes, paints'. Heald adds 'a considerable quantity of provisions which we could not take away with us.' Hull's order said the goods could go to those 'desirous of Escorting you on to Fort Wayne'. What Heald keeps back, the guns, the powder and the whiskey, is what matters most to everyone watching. That night, inside the walls, Heald does something he hopes no one will notice.

stage.caption: Watch the soldiers carry the powder and the whiskey down the covered way to the river.

stops.text: 13 August, evening, from above. A covered way runs from the fort's north-east corner down to the river. 'The same evening the ammunition and liquor were carried, part into the sally-port, and thrown into a well'. Muskets are broken up and dropped in after them. The rest of the liquor goes 'as secretly as possible through the northern gate, the heads of the barrels knocked in, and the contents poured into the river.' Heald feared they 'would make bad use of it'. It is not secret: the knocking carries, and 'the taste of the water the next morning was, as one expressed it, "strong grog."' By morning the river tastes of whiskey, and a rider from Fort Wayne is nearly at the gate.

stage.caption: Watch Wells come in with his Miami escort, and Black Partridge come to hand back his medal.

stops.text: 14 August, sunset, at the main gate. Captain William Wells rides in from Fort Wayne with a Miami escort, Heald says 'about 30 Miamies'. Wells is Rebekah Heald's uncle; he has come to bring her and her husband out, but Wau-Bun says 'all too late'. That evening Black Partridge, a Potawatomi leader from the Illinois River, comes to Heald's quarters and hands back his peace medal: 'I will not wear a token of peace while I am compelled to act as an enemy.' It is the plainest warning anyone gives. At nine tomorrow the gate will open, and everyone inside will walk out of it.

stage.caption: Watch the column come down from the fort and pass you: Wells and the Miamis, the band, the regulars, the wagons with the children, the families, the militia.

stops.text: 15 August 1812, nine in the morning. 'On the 15th, at 9 o'clock in the morning, we commenced our march', Heald wrote. Out of the gate, down to the river's mouth here, and south along the beach: Wells and part of the Miami escort in front, then the fifty-four regulars, the wagons with the women and children, and the twelve townsmen of the militia. Wau-Bun says the band played the Dead March, and that Wells 'had blackened his face before leaving the garrison, in token of his impending fate.' The Kinzie family's boat, warned, waits at this river mouth. A mile and a half ahead, behind the sand bank, men are waiting.

stage.caption: Watch the volley from the bank, the soldiers fire and charge, the fighting hand to hand, Mrs. Helm carried to the lake, and the militia cut down at the wagons.

stops.text: About ten, two miles down the beach. Wells comes 'riding furiously back', shouting 'They are about to attack us!' Mrs. Helm remembered: 'Scarcely were the words uttered when a volley was showered from among the sand-hills.' The company fires one round and charges up the bank; 'One man, a veteran of seventy winters, fell as they ascended.' Sergeant Hays, shot 'through the body', drives his bayonet into Nau-non-gee as the chief comes at him with a tomahawk: 'They fell together.' A tomahawk meant for Mrs. Helm's skull 'alighted on my shoulder', she said, before Black Partridge dragged her into the lake. At the wagons the militia are 'cut down to a man', and a young warrior climbs into the baggage wagon and 'tomahawked the children of the entire group.' The dead are scalped; a soldier's daughter later 'saw her father's scalp in the hands of an Indian afterward.'

stage.caption: Watch Wells come to his niece and take her hand, and fall; then Black Bird come out to Heald's last men.

stops.text: About half past ten. Wells, 'shot through the lungs', reaches his niece, Mrs. Heald, and takes her hand: 'Farewell my child.' She saw 'the blood oozing through his nose and mouth.' Pinned when his horse falls, he 'took aim and fired, killing one of them.' Warned that a gun was pointed at his head, he cried 'Shoot away!' A warrior fired, 'the shot being fatal.' He was scalped, and they 'cut his body open' and 'took out his heart'. Mrs. Heald was 'wounded in six places'. Heald gathers his last men on 'a small elevation in the open prarie'. Black Bird comes out and asks him to surrender, 'promising to spare the lives of all the prisoners.' His count: 'twenty-six regulars and all the militia were killed in the action, with two women and twelve children.'

stage.caption: Watch the Kinzies on their green under guard, Kinzie kneeling to Mrs. Heald's wounded arm.

stops.text: 15 August, sunset, at the house of John Kinzie, the trader who sold to the garrison. His family is spared and brought home under guard: 'At their own mansion the family of Mr. Kinzie were closely guarded by their Indian friends.' Mrs. Heald, badly wounded, is ransomed by Kinzie's clerk for a mule, and Kinzie takes a ball from her arm 'with his penknife.' Next day a war party from the Wabash, faces blackened, sit down silent in the parlor. Then Billy Caldwell, the Sauganash, walks in 'with a calm step' and greets them as friends; they ask only for 'some white cotton in which to wrap their dead'. A few doors west, a wounded woman is hiding, and men are searching the houses.

stage.caption: Watch the searchers come to the Ouilmette house and go in, while Mrs. Helm lies hidden.

stops.text: 16 August, morning, while the fort burns. Margaret Helm, Kinzie's stepdaughter and Lieutenant Helm's wife, wounded at the wagons, has been brought here to Ouilmette's house by Black Partridge in 'the ordinary dress of a Frenchwoman of the country'. When searchers come, the family 'raised a large feather bed and placed her under the edge of it, upon the bedstead, with her face to the wall', and Mrs. Bisson sits sewing on the front of the bed. 'I can but die,' said she; 'let them put an end to my misery at once.' The searchers look round 'and left the house.' Quaife doubts the romance, not the rescue.

title: The Battle of Fort Dearborn (18+)
